definition: Pacification means the process of restoring calm and order to an angry person, crowd, or region — unrest brought to an end by persuasion, concession, force, or some mix of the three.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pacification. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pacification should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The trade caravans returned only after the pacification of the river valley — a campaign the veterans who carried it out never spoke of proudly.
Soothing is the mildest rung: a warm word settles one person's ruffled mood for an evening, while pacification sets out to end open unrest across a whole crowd or region.
Mollification is weaker than pacification: it talks one offended person down from real anger, while pacification takes on resistance at full scale — strikes, riots, uprisings.
Subjugation goes further than pacification: pacification stops when order returns, but subjugation breaks the defeated side's power to resist ever again.

Appeasement buys quiet by giving the angry side what it demands — the calm lasts only as long as the gifts do. Pacification is wider: it names the whole effort of restoring order, whatever mix of persuasion, concession, or force that takes.

Conciliation mends a dispute through goodwill — each side softens its claims and the relationship itself is repaired. Pacification is done by an authority to a restive crowd or region, and it counts as complete once quiet returns, mended feelings or not.

Pacification means the process of restoring calm and order to an angry person, crowd, or region — unrest brought to an end by persuasion, concession, force, or some mix of the three.

When bread riots shut the capital's markets for a week, the new prefect tried everything at once: he cut the grain levy, hired the loudest ringleaders onto the docks, and marched patrols through the squares each evening.
By month's end the stalls had reopened — a pacification his critics called half bribery, half intimidation.
Pacification is more precise than calming or peacemaking here because it names the whole managed process of putting unrest to rest — and it stays neutral about means.

The prefect's mix of concessions and patrols is typical: the word promises only that the disturbance ended, not that anyone ended it gently, which is why in histories it so often carries a wary, official ring.

Pacification is the administrator's word for putting unrest to rest, and it is deliberately quiet about method — histories use it warily, sometimes as a euphemism for campaigns that were anything but gentle.
Unlike suppression, which only crushes, pacification aims at restored order and may mix concession with force; unlike appeasement, it does not simply buy calm by granting demands.
For one upset person rather than a restive crowd, plain soothing is the better word.

Okafor asked her class to read the three sentences twice, then handed out the letters.

The letters — from soldiers, traders, and a schoolteacher who lived through that winter — described burned storehouses, negotiated truces, food shipments, and roadblocks, sometimes all in the same month.
By Friday the class had agreed on one thing: restoring calm and order had been the goal, but the tools ran from persuasion to concessions to force, and quiet had not meant content.
One student's essay put it best: the region was calm the way a held breath is calm.
